top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: Background Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is increasingly used in children with pancreatobiliary disease, but pediatric adverse-event estimates remain variable. We updated the evidence on post-ERCP adverse events in children, pooled post-ERCP pancreatitis (PEP) incidence when study-level data allowed, and summarized reported risk factors and prevention strategies. Methods We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of English-language literature published from January 2015 to June 2025 in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. Eligible quantitative analyses included non-overlapping pediatric primary studies reporting extractable numerators and denominators for post-ERCP adverse events. Prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses were used for background comparison and reference checking only. Random-effects meta-analysis of proportions was planned for outcomes with at least three eligible studies. Risk-factor and prevention data were summarized narratively when definitions or adjustment strategies were too heterogeneous for pooling. Results Sixty-five sources were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 15 non-overlapping primary studies contributed extractable PEP numerators and denominators for quantitative synthesis. PEP was the most frequent adverse event, with a pooled incidence of approximately 7.3% (95% CI, 5.1% to 10.4%; I-squared = 83.7%). Study-level PEP percentages, denominator units, and available adverse-event definition or reporting notes are now shown in Table 1. Bleeding was uncommon and perforation was rare but clinically important. Recurrent or chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic duct manipulation, pancreatic contrast injection, sphincterotomy, difficult cannulation, younger age, lower procedural volume, and trainee involvement or operator experience were recurring risk domains, although not all studies reported stratified event counts. Pediatric evidence for NSAIDs and prophylactic pancreatic stenting remains limited compared with adult data, and both strategies require childspecific dosing, equipment selection, and contraindication assessment. ARTICLE IN PRESS Conclusions Pediatric ERCP carries measurable adverse-event risk, particularly PEP. The pooled estimate provides a current benchmark, but heterogeneity and inconsistent reporting limit certainty. Standardized pediatric definitions, non-overlapping reporting, and prospective multicenter datasets are needed. Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251084264. Keywords Children; ERCP; Pancreatobiliary disease; Post-procedural complications; Pancreatitis; Systematic review; Meta-analysis; Patient safety

top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesizes contemporary evidence on post-ERCP complications in children. Prior reviews were used for context, while original pediatric studies served as the primary evidence base. The findings support ERCP as an important diagnostic and therapeutic tool in pediatric pancreatobiliary disease, but they also show that PEP remains the main adverse event requiring prevention, early recognition, and standardized reporting. Consistent with prior reports, PEP was the most commonly reported adverse event. The present pooled estimate was 7.3% (95% CI, 5.1% to 10.4%), with substantial between-study heterogeneity (I-squared = 83.7%). Table 4 compares this estimate with prior pediatric ERCP meta-analyses. Usatin 2016 and Hosseini 2023 reported lower PEP estimates of approximately 3% to 4%, whereas Sun 2022 provided an overall therapeutic ERCP adverse-event benchmark rather than a uniformly extractable PEP-only estimate[4, 5, 13]. The higher estimate in the present review is likely related to the contemporary search window, explicit restriction to nonoverlapping primary studies with extractable PEP numerators and denominators, high-risk therapeutic indications, pancreatic duct manipulation, and retention of the source-specific denominator unit. Standardized adverse-event reporting using established classifications (e.g., Cotton criteria[88]; revised Atlanta criteria[89]) and pediatric-specific definitions is needed for valid cross-study comparisons. Although PEP was the most commonly reported adverse event, less frequent complications such as bleeding and perforation also require attention. Bleeding was generally uncommon (approximately 0.5%) and was most often associated with endoscopic sphincterotomy. Perforation was rare, generally reported below 1%, but its severity justifies careful technique, especially in children with smaller and more delicate duodenal and biliary anatomy. Risk reduction depends on both patient selection and procedural technique. Younger age, prior pancreatitis, and selected genetic predispositions were recurring patient-level risk factors. Procedural factors such as pancreatic duct manipulation (including deep cannulation and pancreatic sphincterotomy), precut papillotomy, and lower operator experience were also associated with higher risk. Individual risk stratification and referral to high-volume pediatric endoscopy centers may reduce avoidable harm[66]. Preventive strategies remain central to reducing post-ERCP morbidity, but pediatric practice requires more detail than simply importing adult ERCP protocols. For PEP, the most actionable measures are careful indication selection, minimizing pancreatic duct manipulation and contrast injection, limiting cannulation attempts, early senior-operator involvement, and selective prophylactic pancreatic stenting when anatomy and expertise make it safe. Stent size and length should be adapted to the child and duct, and NSAID prophylaxis should be individualized by age, weight, renal function, bleeding risk, and local pediatric protocols. For bleeding, perforation, and cholangitis, countermeasures include correction of coagulation abnormalities, careful sphincterotomy, early recognition of perforation, complete biliary drainage, and selective antibiotics when drainage is incomplete or infection risk is high. ARTICLE IN PRESS Selective prophylactic pancreatic stenting may benefit high-risk pediatric cases, but the evidence remains limited. Intravenous hydration may also help when fluid status can be monitored closely[65, 80]. This study has several strengths: a contemporary search strategy, explicit separation of primary studies from prior reviews, rechecking of percentage-derived PEP rows, and a meta-analytic approach restricted to outcomes with extractable non-overlapping data. Limitations remain. Heterogeneity in indications, adverse-event definitions, follow-up windows, and reporting units limited comparison across studies and prevented pooling of several risk-factor and prevention outcomes. Some studies used procedure-level denominators whereas others used patient-level or first-ERCP-per-child denominators; because repeat procedures per child were not consistently reported, these could not be fully harmonized. Selective reporting, incomplete stratified event counts, and overlap among multicenter cohorts may also affect published estimates. Future research should prioritize prospective multicenter pediatric ERCP datasets with standardized adverse-event definitions and consistent reporting of numerators, denominators, follow-up windows, and severity. Pediatric trials or well-designed registries are also needed for prophylactic agents, pancreatic stenting strategies, and child-adapted ERCP equipment.

top_evidence.text: Meta-analysis was conducted only for outcomes reported by at least three non-overlapping primary studies with extractable numerators and denominators. Pooled incidences were estimated using random-effects models for proportions, with variance stabilization for rare events where appropriate. Results were expressed as pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran Q and the I-squared statistic. Heterogeneity was interpreted as low, moderate, substantial, or considerable using conventional thresholds, while acknowledging that I-squared may be unstable in rare-event analyses. We prespecified subgroup exploration by age group, ERCP indication, procedure type, pancreatic duct manipulation or contrast injection, sphincterotomy, and operator or center volume. Formal subgroup meta-analysis was not forced when studies did not provide stratified PEP event counts, because doing so would have required ecological assumptions. These variables were therefore summarized as explanatory domains for heterogeneity and risk. Sensitivity analyses were planned by excluding studies at high risk of bias, studies with unclear adverseevent definitions, and studies with potential cohort overlap. In response to peer review, we also added a post hoc denominator-unit sensitivity summary, separating procedure-level studies from patient-level or first-ERCP-perchild studies and retaining a mixed/unclear category when the source did not permit classification. Risk-factor effect estimates were not pooled when exposure definitions, covariate adjustment, or reporting units differed substantially. These data were summarized narratively and, where appropriate, displayed as reported estimates. ARTICLE IN PRESS Publication bias was assessed visually using funnel plots and statistically using Egger test only for outcomes with at least ten eligible studies. Funnel plots were not generated for rare outcomes with fewer than ten studies because asymmetry tests would be unreliable. All tests were two-sided. For analyses other than Cochran's Q test for heterogeneity, P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For Cochran's Q test, P < 0.10 was considered indicative of potential between-study heterogeneity because this test has limited power when relatively few studies are included. Heterogeneity was interpreted together with I² and τ². AI-assisted tools were used during revision for language editing and formatting checks. The authors verified the data extraction, statistical analyses, interpretation, and final text and take full responsibility for the manuscript.

top_evidence.text: Xin Wang and Hua Liu made the largest contributions to this work. Xin Wang conceived the review question, designed the search and extraction framework, reconstructed the study-level dataset, performed the metaanalysis, generated the figures, and drafted the manuscript. Ruiying Li contributed to literature screening, data extraction, and table preparation. Wenhai Li contributed to source checking, data verification, and synthesis of risk-factor evidence. Peng Huang contributed to statistical checking, figure review, and interpretation of pooled estimates. Hu Yang contributed to clinical interpretation of pediatric surgical and endoscopic findings and revised the manuscript for important intellectual content. Hongxi Guo contributed to quality assessment, supplementary file preparation, and final source verification. Hua Liu supervised the study, refined the study design, resolved disagreements, interpreted the clinical implications, and critically revised the manuscript. All authors read and approved the final manuscript. Funding This work was supported by Scientific Research Projects from Wuhan Municipal Health Commission (WX23A72). Funders played no role in the study design, execution or manuscript writing. Availability of data and materials The reconstructed extraction sheet, verified PEP dataset, analysis script, and figure source data are provided as supplementary files. Additional details are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. Ethics declarations Ethics approval and consent to participate Not applicable. This study is a systematic review and meta-analysis of published data and did not involve new recruitment of human participants or access to identifiable individual patient data. Consent for publication ARTICLE IN PRESS Not applicable.

top_evidence.text: Most included primary studies were retrospective or observational, and the overall certainty of evidence was limited by heterogeneous adverse-event definitions, variable follow-up windows, incomplete reporting of denominators for specific complications, and potential overlap among multicenter pediatric ERCP cohorts. Contemporary multicenter studies generally provided stronger evidence for technical outcomes and common adverse events, whereas estimates for rare events such as perforation and cholangitis were less precise. Prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses were useful for benchmarking but were not used as data sources in the present pooled analyses.

top_evidence.text: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to identify, pool, and stratify reported post-ERCP adverse events in pediatric patients. Two reviewers independently searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for literature on pediatric ERCP complications. Any discrepancies in study selection were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. The search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and free-text keywords using Boolean operators (AND, OR). Keywords included: 'children', 'pediatric', 'ERCP', 'endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography', 'complications', 'adverse event', 'pancreatitis', 'bleeding', 'perforation', and 'infection'. The search was limited to studies published between January 1, 2015, and June 26, 2025, to capture contemporary pediatric ERCP practice, including changes in therapeutic indications, endoscopic accessories, anesthesia support, and prophylaxis strategies. Earlier evidence was considered through prior reviews only for contextual comparison. Reference lists of eligible studies and relevant reviews were manually checked to identify additional contemporary primary studies. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Studies were selected using predefined criteria: Inclusion Criteria: Study Type: Original pediatric studies, including cohort studies, case-control studies, and randomized or nonrandomized interventional studies. Prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses were screened for contextual comparison and citation tracking only. Their pooled results were not entered into the present quantitative synthesis. Population: Pediatric patients (<18 years) undergoing ERCP. Outcomes: Reported incidence, types, risk factors, or management strategies of post-ERCP complications. Language: English. Publication Date: January 1, 2015 to June 26, 2025. ARTICLE IN PRESS Exclusion Criteria: Population: Adult patients (≥18 years). Intervention: Research unrelated to ERCP complications. Study Design: Case reports, narrative reviews, editorials, conference abstracts, animal studies, in vitro studies. Data Availability: Incomplete or unextractable data. Duplication: Repeated publications.

top_evidence.text: Meta-analysis was conducted only for outcomes reported by at least three non-overlapping primary studies with extractable numerators and denominators. Pooled incidences were estimated using random-effects models for proportions, with variance stabilization for rare events where appropriate. Results were expressed as pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran Q and the I-squared statistic. Heterogeneity was interpreted as low, moderate, substantial, or considerable using conventional thresholds, while acknowledging that I-squared may be unstable in rare-event analyses. We prespecified subgroup exploration by age group, ERCP indication, procedure type, pancreatic duct manipulation or contrast injection, sphincterotomy, and operator or center volume. Formal subgroup meta-analysis was not forced when studies did not provide stratified PEP event counts, because doing so would have required ecological assumptions. These variables were therefore summarized as explanatory domains for heterogeneity and risk. Sensitivity analyses were planned by excluding studies at high risk of bias, studies with unclear adverseevent definitions, and studies with potential cohort overlap. In response to peer review, we also added a post hoc denominator-unit sensitivity summary, separating procedure-level studies from patient-level or first-ERCP-perchild studies and retaining a mixed/unclear category when the source did not permit classification. Risk-factor effect estimates were not pooled when exposure definitions, covariate adjustment, or reporting units differed substantially. These data were summarized narratively and, where appropriate, displayed as reported estimates. ARTICLE IN PRESS Publication bias was assessed visually using funnel plots and statistically using Egger test only for outcomes with at least ten eligible studies. Funnel plots were not generated for rare outcomes with fewer than ten studies because asymmetry tests would be unreliable. All tests were two-sided. For analyses other than Cochran's Q test for heterogeneity, P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For Cochran's Q test, P < 0.10 was considered indicative of potential between-study heterogeneity because this test has limited power when relatively few studies are included. Heterogeneity was interpreted together with I² and τ². AI-assisted tools were used during revision for language editing and formatting checks. The authors verified the data extraction, statistical analyses, interpretation, and final text and take full responsibility for the manuscript.

top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: The available evidence suggested that ERCP indication influenced complication patterns. Children undergoing ERCP for acute recurrent or chronic pancreatitis were repeatedly reported to have higher PEP risk than those undergoing ERCP for choledocholithiasis, although the magnitude of association varied by study design, adjustment strategy, and procedural case mix. The overall incidence of post-ERCP complications in children varied across studies because of differences in patient populations, procedural indications, adverse-event definitions, and follow-up. Random-effects pooling was performed for PEP because this outcome had the most consistently extractable numerators and denominators. Figure 2 presents the study-level forest plot for PEP incidence after pediatric ERCP. Bleeding, perforation, and cholangitis were less frequent and were summarized descriptively when study-level event data were sparse or inconsistently reported. PEP : PEP was the most frequent and clinically significant complication associated with pediatric ERCP. In the present synthesis, 15 non-overlapping primary studies contributed extractable PEP event counts, yielding a pooled incidence of 7.3% (95% CI, 5.1% to 10.4%; I-squared = 83.7%) under a random-effects model. Table 1 now reports the study-level numerator, denominator, percentage, denominator unit, and available definition or reporting note for every study contributing to the PEP synthesis. The rows most dependent on percentage backcalculation or source-unit interpretation were rechecked against the original source records for Goetz, Mercier, Perera, and Batibay[24, 60, 63, 72]. ARTICLE IN PRESS The high I-squared value indicates real between-study inconsistency rather than a single uniform pediatric PEP risk. Likely contributors include age distribution, acute recurrent or chronic pancreatitis as the indication, pancreatic duct cannulation or contrast injection, pancreatic sphincterotomy, difficult cannulation, operator and center volume, trainee participation, follow-up windows, and differences in PEP definitions. Denominator unit was another source of variation: some studies reported ERCP procedures, whereas others reported patients or first ERCP per child. Because repeat ERCPs per child were not consistently available, procedure-level data were not converted to patient-level data. In the post hoc denominator-unit summary, procedure-level studies contributed 181 PEP events among 2669 ERCPs (crude rate, 6.8%), patient-level or first-ERCP-per-child studies contributed 20 events among 421 children (4.8%), and the mixed or unclear-denominator study contributed 12 events among 232 observations (5.2%). Heterogeneity persisted after this separation, so the pooled estimate should be interpreted as a contemporary benchmark rather than a single individualized risk estimate. Most pediatric PEP cases are mild and resolve with conservative management, whereas a minority progress to moderate or severe PEP with prolonged hospitalization, systemic inflammatory response, pancreatic necrosis, pseudocyst formation, or rarely mortality[4, 59, 73]. The Atlanta classification, originally developed for adults, is often applied in pediatric settings but has not been fully validated for pediatric post-ERCP pathophysiology [62]. Visual inspection of the PEP funnel plot suggested possible small-study effects, although Egger regression did not show clear statistical evidence of asymmetry (intercept, -1.98; approximate two-sided P = 0.16). This result should be interpreted cautiously because heterogeneity was substantial and denominators were reported as either patients or procedures across studies (Figure 8). Bleeding : Post-ERCP bleeding in children most commonly occurs after endoscopic sphincterotomy (EST). Clinically significant bleeding is uncommon, with an estimated incidence of approximately 0.5%[4]. Bleeding may appear during the procedure, shortly afterward, or several days later. Reported risk factors include coagulopathy, larger sphincterotomy incisions, and vascular anomalies. Most cases respond to endoscopic hemostasis with epinephrine injection or clip placement. Severe or endoscopically refractory bleeding may require angiographic embolization; surgery should be reserved for cases in which less invasive measures fail. Perforation : ERCP-related perforation is rare but potentially life-threatening, with an estimated incidence below 1% in pediatric patients[4]. Risk factors include difficult cannulation, excessive force during guidewire or endoscope advancement, anatomical anomalies, and strictures. A practical concern is device size. Pediatric duodenoscopes have become less available in recent years, so clinicians may need to use adult-sized equipment in small children, which can increase mechanical risk. Early recognition matters: minor perforations may be treated conservatively, whereas larger defects often require surgery. Cholangitis : Post-ERCP cholangitis is a recognized infectious complication, typically resulting from incomplete biliary drainage or procedural contamination. Although its incidence in children is less well-defined than that of PEP, it remains clinically important[63]. Risk factors include persistent biliary obstruction, incomplete stone clearance, and prior biliary surgery. Prophylactic antibiotics are commonly considered, particularly in patients with pre-existing cholangitis or immunocompromised status. Management requires prompt antibiotic therapy and restoration of biliary drainage, which may require repeat ERCP or percutaneous intervention. Other complications : Less common complications of ERCP in children include cholecystitis, bile duct injury or stricture, and events related to sedation or anesthesia[13]. Cholecystitis may arise if the cystic duct is obstructed or manipulated during the procedure. Ductal injury is rare but can lead to later stricture formation. Sedation- and anesthesia-related complications are especially relevant in children because of smaller airway size, higher metabolic demand, and age-specific responses to anesthetic agents. Close monitoring by pediatric anesthesia teams is therefore important for procedural safety[64]. The evidence points to a broad but unevenly reported risk profile for pediatric ERCP. Overall complication rates are usually low, but serious events such as PEP, bleeding, perforation, and cholangitis require close attention. Differences in definitions, follow-up, and reporting explain much of the variability across studies. Better pediatric definitions and prospective datasets are needed before risk estimates for rare outcomes can be pooled with confidence. Risk Factors for Complications Operator background also influenced complication rates. Pediatric series and adult operator-volume data[66, 68, 69] suggest that procedures performed by less experienced operators or outside specialized pediatric endoscopy settings may carry higher procedural risk than procedures performed by experienced pediatric gastroenterologists. These findings support specialized training and referral pathways for complex pediatric ERCP. ARTICLE IN PRESS Identifying risk factors for post-ERCP complications in children helps guide patient selection, preprocedural optimization, and intra-procedural risk mitigation. Across the literature, both patient characteristics and procedural variables were associated with adverse events. Table 2 summarizes major patient- and procedure-related factors associated with higher complication rates, particularly PEP, bleeding, and perforation. To complement this summary, Figure 3 summarizes patient-related and procedure-related risk domains reported across the included literature.

top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to identify, pool, and stratify reported post-ERCP adverse events in pediatric patients. Two reviewers independently searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for literature on pediatric ERCP complications. Any discrepancies in study selection were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. The search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and free-text keywords using Boolean operators (AND, OR). Keywords included: 'children', 'pediatric', 'ERCP', 'endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography', 'complications', 'adverse event', 'pancreatitis', 'bleeding', 'perforation', and 'infection'. The search was limited to studies published between January 1, 2015, and June 26, 2025, to capture contemporary pediatric ERCP practice, including changes in therapeutic indications, endoscopic accessories, anesthesia support, and prophylaxis strategies. Earlier evidence was considered through prior reviews only for contextual comparison. Reference lists of eligible studies and relevant reviews were manually checked to identify additional contemporary primary studies. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Studies were selected using predefined criteria: Inclusion Criteria: Study Type: Original pediatric studies, including cohort studies, case-control studies, and randomized or nonrandomized interventional studies. Prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses were screened for contextual comparison and citation tracking only. Their pooled results were not entered into the present quantitative synthesis. Population: Pediatric patients (<18 years) undergoing ERCP. Outcomes: Reported incidence, types, risk factors, or management strategies of post-ERCP complications. Language: English. Publication Date: January 1, 2015 to June 26, 2025. ARTICLE IN PRESS Exclusion Criteria: Population: Adult patients (≥18 years). Intervention: Research unrelated to ERCP complications. Study Design: Case reports, narrative reviews, editorials, conference abstracts, animal studies, in vitro studies. Data Availability: Incomplete or unextractable data. Duplication: Repeated publications.

top_evidence.text: Meta-analysis was conducted only for outcomes reported by at least three non-overlapping primary studies with extractable numerators and denominators. Pooled incidences were estimated using random-effects models for proportions, with variance stabilization for rare events where appropriate. Results were expressed as pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran Q and the I-squared statistic. Heterogeneity was interpreted as low, moderate, substantial, or considerable using conventional thresholds, while acknowledging that I-squared may be unstable in rare-event analyses. We prespecified subgroup exploration by age group, ERCP indication, procedure type, pancreatic duct manipulation or contrast injection, sphincterotomy, and operator or center volume. Formal subgroup meta-analysis was not forced when studies did not provide stratified PEP event counts, because doing so would have required ecological assumptions. These variables were therefore summarized as explanatory domains for heterogeneity and risk. Sensitivity analyses were planned by excluding studies at high risk of bias, studies with unclear adverseevent definitions, and studies with potential cohort overlap. In response to peer review, we also added a post hoc denominator-unit sensitivity summary, separating procedure-level studies from patient-level or first-ERCP-perchild studies and retaining a mixed/unclear category when the source did not permit classification. Risk-factor effect estimates were not pooled when exposure definitions, covariate adjustment, or reporting units differed substantially. These data were summarized narratively and, where appropriate, displayed as reported estimates. ARTICLE IN PRESS Publication bias was assessed visually using funnel plots and statistically using Egger test only for outcomes with at least ten eligible studies. Funnel plots were not generated for rare outcomes with fewer than ten studies because asymmetry tests would be unreliable. All tests were two-sided. For analyses other than Cochran's Q test for heterogeneity, P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For Cochran's Q test, P < 0.10 was considered indicative of potential between-study heterogeneity because this test has limited power when relatively few studies are included. Heterogeneity was interpreted together with I² and τ². AI-assisted tools were used during revision for language editing and formatting checks. top_evidence.text: The methodological quality and risk of bias of each eligible source were independently assessed by two reviewers using tools appropriate to study design. Disagreements were resolved by consensus, with a third reviewer consulted when needed. Non-randomized primary studies were assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), randomized trials using RoB 2, and prior systematic reviews or meta-analyses using AMSTAR 2[16-18]. Rather than reproducing checklist content, we summarized each study's overall judgment and used these judgments to grade confidence across evidence domains. Risk-of-bias judgments informed the narrative synthesis. Studies with incomplete adverse-event definitions, unclear denominators, overlapping cohorts, or high risk of selection or reporting bias were interpreted cautiously and were not used to support quantitative claims beyond their reported data.

top_evidence.text: The available evidence suggested that ERCP indication influenced complication patterns. Children undergoing ERCP for acute recurrent or chronic pancreatitis were repeatedly reported to have higher PEP risk than those undergoing ERCP for choledocholithiasis, although the magnitude of association varied by study design, adjustment strategy, and procedural case mix. The overall incidence of post-ERCP complications in children varied across studies because of differences in patient populations, procedural indications, adverse-event definitions, and follow-up. Random-effects pooling was performed for PEP because this outcome had the most consistently extractable numerators and denominators. Figure 2 presents the study-level forest plot for PEP incidence after pediatric ERCP. Bleeding, perforation, and cholangitis were less frequent and were summarized descriptively when study-level event data were sparse or inconsistently reported. PEP : PEP was the most frequent and clinically significant complication associated with pediatric ERCP. In the present synthesis, 15 non-overlapping primary studies contributed extractable PEP event counts, yielding a pooled incidence of 7.3% (95% CI, 5.1% to 10.4%; I-squared = 83.7%) under a random-effects model. Table 1 now reports the study-level numerator, denominator, percentage, denominator unit, and available definition or reporting note for every study contributing to the PEP synthesis. The rows most dependent on percentage backcalculation or source-unit interpretation were rechecked against the original source records for Goetz, Mercier, Perera, and Batibay[24, 60, 63, 72]. ARTICLE IN PRESS The high I-squared value indicates real between-study inconsistency rather than a single uniform pediatric PEP risk. Likely contributors include age distribution, acute recurrent or chronic pancreatitis as the indication, pancreatic duct cannulation or contrast injection, pancreatic sphincterotomy, difficult cannulation, operator and center volume, trainee participation, follow-up windows, and differences in PEP definitions. Denominator unit was another source of variation: some studies reported ERCP procedures, whereas others reported patients or first ERCP per child. Because repeat ERCPs per child were not consistently available, procedure-level data were not converted to patient-level data. In the post hoc denominator-unit summary, procedure-level studies contributed 181 PEP events among 2669 ERCPs (crude rate, 6.8%), patient-level or first-ERCP-per-child studies contributed 20 events among 421 children (4.8%), and the mixed or unclear-denominator study contributed 12 events among 232 observations (5.2%). Heterogeneity persisted after this separation, so the pooled estimate should be interpreted as a contemporary benchmark rather than a single individualized risk estimate. Most pediatric PEP cases are mild and resolve with conservative management, whereas a minority progress to moderate or severe PEP with prolonged hospitalization, systemic inflammatory response, pancreatic necrosis, pseudocyst formation, or rarely mortality[4, 59, 73]. The Atlanta classification, originally developed for adults, is often applied in pediatric settings but has not been fully validated for pediatric post-ERCP pathophysiology [62]. Visual inspection of the PEP funnel plot suggested possible small-study effects, although Egger regression did not show clear statistical evidence of asymmetry (intercept, -1.98; approximate two-sided P = 0.16). This result should be interpreted cautiously because heterogeneity was substantial and denominators were reported as either patients or procedures across studies (Figure 8). Bleeding : Post-ERCP bleeding in children most commonly occurs after endoscopic sphincterotomy (EST). Clinically significant bleeding is uncommon, with an estimated incidence of approximately 0.5%[4]. Bleeding may appear during the procedure, shortly afterward, or several days later. Reported risk factors include coagulopathy, larger sphincterotomy incisions, and vascular anomalies. Most cases respond to endoscopic hemostasis with epinephrine injection or clip placement. Severe or endoscopically refractory bleeding may require angiographic embolization; surgery should be reserved for cases in which less invasive measures fail. Perforation : ERCP-related perforation is rare but potentially life-threatening, with an estimated incidence below 1% in pediatric patients[4]. Risk factors include difficult cannulation, excessive force during guidewire or endoscope advancement, anatomical anomalies, and strictures. A practical concern is device size. Pediatric duodenoscopes have become less available in recent years, so clinicians may need to use adult-sized equipment in small children, which can increase mechanical risk. Early recognition matters: minor perforations may be treated conservatively, whereas larger defects often require surgery. Cholangitis : Post-ERCP cholangitis is a recognized infectious complication, typically resulting from incomplete biliary drainage or procedural contamination. Although its incidence in children is less well-defined than that of PEP, it remains clinically important[63]. Risk factors include persistent biliary obstruction, incomplete stone clearance, and prior biliary surgery. Prophylactic antibiotics are commonly considered, particularly in patients with pre-existing cholangitis or immunocompromised status. Management requires prompt antibiotic therapy and restoration of biliary drainage, which may require repeat ERCP or percutaneous intervention. Other complications : Less common complications of ERCP in children include cholecystitis, bile duct injury or stricture, and events related to sedation or anesthesia[13]. Cholecystitis may arise if the cystic duct is obstructed or manipulated during the procedure. Ductal injury is rare but can lead to later stricture formation. Sedation- and anesthesia-related complications are especially relevant in children because of smaller airway size, higher metabolic demand, and age-specific responses to anesthetic agents. Close monitoring by pediatric anesthesia teams is therefore important for procedural safety[64]. The evidence points to a broad but unevenly reported risk profile for pediatric ERCP. Overall complication rates are usually low, but serious events such as PEP, bleeding, perforation, and cholangitis require close attention. Differences in definitions, follow-up, and reporting explain much of the variability across studies. Better pediatric definitions and prospective datasets are needed before risk estimates for rare outcomes can be pooled with confidence. Risk Factors for Complications Operator background also influenced complication rates. Pediatric series and adult operator-volume data[66, 68, 69] suggest that procedures performed by less experienced operators or outside specialized pediatric endoscopy settings may carry higher procedural risk than procedures performed by experienced pediatric gastroenterologists. These findings support specialized training and referral pathways for complex pediatric ERCP. ARTICLE IN PRESS Identifying risk factors for post-ERCP complications in children helps guide patient selection, preprocedural optimization, and intra-procedural risk mitigation. Across the literature, both patient characteristics and procedural variables were associated with adverse events. Table 2 summarizes major patient- and procedure-related factors associated with higher complication rates, particularly PEP, bleeding, and perforation. To complement this summary, Figure 3 summarizes patient-related and procedure-related risk domains reported across the included literature.

top_evidence.text: Most included primary studies were retrospective or observational, and the overall certainty of evidence was limited by heterogeneous adverse-event definitions, variable follow-up windows, incomplete reporting of denominators for specific complications, and potential overlap among multicenter pediatric ERCP cohorts. Contemporary multicenter studies generally provided stronger evidence for technical outcomes and common adverse events, whereas estimates for rare events such as perforation and cholangitis were less precise. Prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses were useful for benchmarking but were not used as data sources in the present pooled analyses.

top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: Background Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is increasingly used in children with pancreatobiliary disease, but pediatric adverse-event estimates remain variable. We updated the evidence on post-ERCP adverse events in children, pooled post-ERCP pancreatitis (PEP) incidence when study-level data allowed, and summarized reported risk factors and prevention strategies. Methods We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of English-language literature published from January 2015 to June 2025 in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. Eligible quantitative analyses included non-overlapping pediatric primary studies reporting extractable numerators and denominators for post-ERCP adverse events. Prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses were used for background comparison and reference checking only. Random-effects meta-analysis of proportions was planned for outcomes with at least three eligible studies. Risk-factor and prevention data were summarized narratively when definitions or adjustment strategies were too heterogeneous for pooling. Results Sixty-five sources were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 15 non-overlapping primary studies contributed extractable PEP numerators and denominators for quantitative synthesis. PEP was the most frequent adverse event, with a pooled incidence of approximately 7.3% (95% CI, 5.1% to 10.4%; I-squared = 83.7%). Study-level PEP percentages, denominator units, and available adverse-event definition or reporting notes are now shown in Table 1. Bleeding was uncommon and perforation was rare but clinically important. Recurrent or chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic duct manipulation, pancreatic contrast injection, sphincterotomy, difficult cannulation, younger age, lower procedural volume, and trainee involvement or operator experience were recurring risk domains, although not all studies reported stratified event counts. Pediatric evidence for NSAIDs and prophylactic pancreatic stenting remains limited compared with adult data, and both strategies require childspecific dosing, equipment selection, and contraindication assessment. ARTICLE IN PRESS Conclusions Pediatric ERCP carries measurable adverse-event risk, particularly PEP. The pooled estimate provides a current benchmark, but heterogeneity and inconsistent reporting limit certainty. Standardized pediatric definitions, non-overlapping reporting, and prospective multicenter datasets are needed. Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251084264. Heterogeneity was interpreted as low, moderate, substantial, or considerable using conventional thresholds, while acknowledging that I-squared may be unstable in rare-event analyses. Formal subgroup meta-analysis was not forced when studies did not provide stratified PEP event counts, because doing so would have required ecological assumptions. These variables were therefore summarized as explanatory domains for heterogeneity and risk. Sensitivity analyses were planned by excluding studies at high risk of bias, studies with unclear adverseevent definitions, and studies with potential cohort overlap. In response to peer review, we also added a post hoc denominator-unit sensitivity summary, separating procedure-level studies from patient-level or first-ERCP-perchild studies and retaining a mixed/unclear category when the source did not permit classification. Risk-factor effect estimates were not pooled when exposure definitions, covariate adjustment, or reporting units differed substantially. These data were summarized narratively and, where appropriate, displayed as reported estimates. top_evidence.text: The available evidence suggested that ERCP indication influenced complication patterns. Children undergoing ERCP for acute recurrent or chronic pancreatitis were repeatedly reported to have higher PEP risk than those undergoing ERCP for choledocholithiasis, although the magnitude of association varied by study design, adjustment strategy, and procedural case mix. The overall incidence of post-ERCP complications in children varied across studies because of differences in patient populations, procedural indications, adverse-event definitions, and follow-up. Random-effects pooling was performed for PEP because this outcome had the most consistently extractable numerators and denominators. Figure 2 presents the study-level forest plot for PEP incidence after pediatric ERCP. Bleeding, perforation, and cholangitis were less frequent and were summarized descriptively when study-level event data were sparse or inconsistently reported. PEP : PEP was the most frequent and clinically significant complication associated with pediatric ERCP. In the present synthesis, 15 non-overlapping primary studies contributed extractable PEP event counts, yielding a pooled incidence of 7.3% (95% CI, 5.1% to 10.4%; I-squared = 83.7%) under a random-effects model. Table 1 now reports the study-level numerator, denominator, percentage, denominator unit, and available definition or reporting note for every study contributing to the PEP synthesis. The rows most dependent on percentage backcalculation or source-unit interpretation were rechecked against the original source records for Goetz, Mercier, Perera, and Batibay[24, 60, 63, 72]. ARTICLE IN PRESS The high I-squared value indicates real between-study inconsistency rather than a single uniform pediatric PEP risk. Likely contributors include age distribution, acute recurrent or chronic pancreatitis as the indication, pancreatic duct cannulation or contrast injection, pancreatic sphincterotomy, difficult cannulation, operator and center volume, trainee participation, follow-up windows, and differences in PEP definitions. Denominator unit was another source of variation: some studies reported ERCP procedures, whereas others reported patients or first ERCP per child. Because repeat ERCPs per child were not consistently available, procedure-level data were not converted to patient-level data. In the post hoc denominator-unit summary, procedure-level studies contributed 181 PEP events among 2669 ERCPs (crude rate, 6.8%), patient-level or first-ERCP-per-child studies contributed 20 events among 421 children (4.8%), and the mixed or unclear-denominator study contributed 12 events among 232 observations (5.2%). Heterogeneity persisted after this separation, so the pooled estimate should be interpreted as a contemporary benchmark rather than a single individualized risk estimate. Most pediatric PEP cases are mild and resolve with conservative management, whereas a minority progress to moderate or severe PEP with prolonged hospitalization, systemic inflammatory response, pancreatic necrosis, pseudocyst formation, or rarely mortality[4, 59, 73]. The Atlanta classification, originally developed for adults, is often applied in pediatric settings but has not been fully validated for pediatric post-ERCP pathophysiology [62]. Visual inspection of the PEP funnel plot suggested possible small-study effects, although Egger regression did not show clear statistical evidence of asymmetry (intercept, -1.98; approximate two-sided P = 0.16). This result should be interpreted cautiously because heterogeneity was substantial and denominators were reported as either patients or procedures across studies (Figure 8). Bleeding : Post-ERCP bleeding in children most commonly occurs after endoscopic sphincterotomy (EST). Clinically significant bleeding is uncommon, with an estimated incidence of approximately 0.5%[4]. Bleeding may appear during the procedure, shortly afterward, or several days later. Reported risk factors include coagulopathy, larger sphincterotomy incisions, and vascular anomalies. Most cases respond to endoscopic hemostasis with epinephrine injection or clip placement. Severe or endoscopically refractory bleeding may require angiographic embolization; surgery should be reserved for cases in which less invasive measures fail. Perforation : ERCP-related perforation is rare but potentially life-threatening, with an estimated incidence below 1% in pediatric patients[4]. Risk factors include difficult cannulation, excessive force during guidewire or endoscope advancement, anatomical anomalies, and strictures. A practical concern is device size. Pediatric duodenoscopes have become less available in recent years, so clinicians may need to use adult-sized equipment in small children, which can increase mechanical risk. Early recognition matters: minor perforations may be treated conservatively, whereas larger defects often require surgery. Cholangitis : Post-ERCP cholangitis is a recognized infectious complication, typically resulting from incomplete biliary drainage or procedural contamination. Although its incidence in children is less well-defined than that of PEP, it remains clinically important[63]. Risk factors include persistent biliary obstruction, incomplete stone clearance, and prior biliary surgery. Prophylactic antibiotics are commonly considered, particularly in patients with pre-existing cholangitis or immunocompromised status. Management requires prompt antibiotic therapy and restoration of biliary drainage, which may require repeat ERCP or percutaneous intervention. Other complications : Less common complications of ERCP in children include cholecystitis, bile duct injury or stricture, and events related to sedation or anesthesia[13]. Cholecystitis may arise if the cystic duct is obstructed or manipulated during the procedure. Ductal injury is rare but can lead to later stricture formation. Sedation- and anesthesia-related complications are especially relevant in children because of smaller airway size, higher metabolic demand, and age-specific responses to anesthetic agents. Close monitoring by pediatric anesthesia teams is therefore important for procedural safety[64]. The evidence points to a broad but unevenly reported risk profile for pediatric ERCP. Overall complication rates are usually low, but serious events such as PEP, bleeding, perforation, and cholangitis require close attention. Differences in definitions, follow-up, and reporting explain much of the variability across studies. Better pediatric definitions and prospective datasets are needed before risk estimates for rare outcomes can be pooled with confidence. Risk Factors for Complications Operator background also influenced complication rates. Pediatric series and adult operator-volume data[66, 68, 69] suggest that procedures performed by less experienced operators or outside specialized pediatric endoscopy settings may carry higher procedural risk than procedures performed by experienced pediatric gastroenterologists. These findings support specialized training and referral pathways for complex pediatric ERCP. ARTICLE IN PRESS Identifying risk factors for post-ERCP complications in children helps guide patient selection, preprocedural optimization, and intra-procedural risk mitigation. Across the literature, both patient characteristics and procedural variables were associated with adverse events. Table 2 summarizes major patient- and procedure-related factors associated with higher complication rates, particularly PEP, bleeding, and perforation. To complement this summary, Figure 3 summarizes patient-related and procedure-related risk domains reported across the included literature.

top_evidence.text: Background Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is increasingly used in children with pancreatobiliary disease, but pediatric adverse-event estimates remain variable. We updated the evidence on post-ERCP adverse events in children, pooled post-ERCP pancreatitis (PEP) incidence when study-level data allowed, and summarized reported risk factors and prevention strategies. Methods We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of English-language literature published from January 2015 to June 2025 in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. Eligible quantitative analyses included non-overlapping pediatric primary studies reporting extractable numerators and denominators for post-ERCP adverse events. Prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses were used for background comparison and reference checking only. Random-effects meta-analysis of proportions was planned for outcomes with at least three eligible studies. Risk-factor and prevention data were summarized narratively when definitions or adjustment strategies were too heterogeneous for pooling. Results Sixty-five sources were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 15 non-overlapping primary studies contributed extractable PEP numerators and denominators for quantitative synthesis. PEP was the most frequent adverse event, with a pooled incidence of approximately 7.3% (95% CI, 5.1% to 10.4%; I-squared = 83.7%). Study-level PEP percentages, denominator units, and available adverse-event definition or reporting notes are now shown in Table 1. Bleeding was uncommon and perforation was rare but clinically important. Recurrent or chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic duct manipulation, pancreatic contrast injection, sphincterotomy, difficult cannulation, younger age, lower procedural volume, and trainee involvement or operator experience were recurring risk domains, although not all studies reported stratified event counts. Pediatric evidence for NSAIDs and prophylactic pancreatic stenting remains limited compared with adult data, and both strategies require childspecific dosing, equipment selection, and contraindication assessment. ARTICLE IN PRESS Conclusions Pediatric ERCP carries measurable adverse-event risk, particularly PEP. The pooled estimate provides a current benchmark, but heterogeneity and inconsistent reporting limit certainty. Standardized pediatric definitions, non-overlapping reporting, and prospective multicenter datasets are needed. Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251084264. Keywords Children; ERCP; Pancreatobiliary disease; Post-procedural complications; Pancreatitis; Systematic review; Meta-analysis; Patient safety

top_evidence.text: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to identify, pool, and stratify reported post-ERCP adverse events in pediatric patients. Two reviewers independently searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for literature on pediatric ERCP complications. Any discrepancies in study selection were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. The search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and free-text keywords using Boolean operators (AND, OR). Keywords included: 'children', 'pediatric', 'ERCP', 'endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography', 'complications', 'adverse event', 'pancreatitis', 'bleeding', 'perforation', and 'infection'. The search was limited to studies published between January 1, 2015, and June 26, 2025, to capture contemporary pediatric ERCP practice, including changes in therapeutic indications, endoscopic accessories, anesthesia support, and prophylaxis strategies. Earlier evidence was considered through prior reviews only for contextual comparison. Reference lists of eligible studies and relevant reviews were manually checked to identify additional contemporary primary studies. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Studies were selected using predefined criteria: Inclusion Criteria: Study Type: Original pediatric studies, including cohort studies, case-control studies, and randomized or nonrandomized interventional studies. Prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses were screened for contextual comparison and citation tracking only. Their pooled results were not entered into the present quantitative synthesis. Population: Pediatric patients (<18 years) undergoing ERCP. Outcomes: Reported incidence, types, risk factors, or management strategies of post-ERCP complications. Language: English. Publication Date: January 1, 2015 to June 26, 2025. ARTICLE IN PRESS Exclusion Criteria: Population: Adult patients (≥18 years). Intervention: Research unrelated to ERCP complications. Study Design: Case reports, narrative reviews, editorials, conference abstracts, animal studies, in vitro studies. Data Availability: Incomplete or unextractable data. Duplication: Repeated publications.

top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: Background Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is increasingly used in children with pancreatobiliary disease, but pediatric adverse-event estimates remain variable. We updated the evidence on post-ERCP adverse events in children, pooled post-ERCP pancreatitis (PEP) incidence when study-level data allowed, and summarized reported risk factors and prevention strategies. Methods We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of English-language literature published from January 2015 to June 2025 in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. Eligible quantitative analyses included non-overlapping pediatric primary studies reporting extractable numerators and denominators for post-ERCP adverse events. Prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses were used for background comparison and reference checking only. Random-effects meta-analysis of proportions was planned for outcomes with at least three eligible studies. Risk-factor and prevention data were summarized narratively when definitions or adjustment strategies were too heterogeneous for pooling. Results Sixty-five sources were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 15 non-overlapping primary studies contributed extractable PEP numerators and denominators for quantitative synthesis. PEP was the most frequent adverse event, with a pooled incidence of approximately 7.3% (95% CI, 5.1% to 10.4%; I-squared = 83.7%). Study-level PEP percentages, denominator units, and available adverse-event definition or reporting notes are now shown in Table 1. Bleeding was uncommon and perforation was rare but clinically important. Recurrent or chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic duct manipulation, pancreatic contrast injection, sphincterotomy, difficult cannulation, younger age, lower procedural volume, and trainee involvement or operator experience were recurring risk domains, although not all studies reported stratified event counts. Pediatric evidence for NSAIDs and prophylactic pancreatic stenting remains limited compared with adult data, and both strategies require childspecific dosing, equipment selection, and contraindication assessment. ARTICLE IN PRESS Conclusions Pediatric ERCP carries measurable adverse-event risk, particularly PEP. The pooled estimate provides a current benchmark, but heterogeneity and inconsistent reporting limit certainty. Standardized pediatric definitions, non-overlapping reporting, and prospective multicenter datasets are needed. Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251084264. Keywords Children; ERCP; Pancreatobiliary disease; Post-procedural complications; Pancreatitis; Systematic review; Meta-analysis; Patient safety

top_evidence.text: Meta-analysis was conducted only for outcomes reported by at least three non-overlapping primary studies with extractable numerators and denominators. Pooled incidences were estimated using random-effects models for proportions, with variance stabilization for rare events where appropriate. Results were expressed as pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran Q and the I-squared statistic. Heterogeneity was interpreted as low, moderate, substantial, or considerable using conventional thresholds, while acknowledging that I-squared may be unstable in rare-event analyses. We prespecified subgroup exploration by age group, ERCP indication, procedure type, pancreatic duct manipulation or contrast injection, sphincterotomy, and operator or center volume. Formal subgroup meta-analysis was not forced when studies did not provide stratified PEP event counts, because doing so would have required ecological assumptions. These variables were therefore summarized as explanatory domains for heterogeneity and risk. Sensitivity analyses were planned by excluding studies at high risk of bias, studies with unclear adverseevent definitions, and studies with potential cohort overlap. In response to peer review, we also added a post hoc denominator-unit sensitivity summary, separating procedure-level studies from patient-level or first-ERCP-perchild studies and retaining a mixed/unclear category when the source did not permit classification. Risk-factor effect estimates were not pooled when exposure definitions, covariate adjustment, or reporting units differed substantially. These data were summarized narratively and, where appropriate, displayed as reported estimates. ARTICLE IN PRESS Publication bias was assessed visually using funnel plots and statistically using Egger test only for outcomes with at least ten eligible studies. Funnel plots were not generated for rare outcomes with fewer than ten studies because asymmetry tests would be unreliable. All tests were two-sided. For analyses other than Cochran's Q test for heterogeneity, P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For Cochran's Q test, P < 0.10 was considered indicative of potential between-study heterogeneity because this test has limited power when relatively few studies are included. Heterogeneity was interpreted together with I² and τ². AI-assisted tools were used during revision for language editing and formatting checks. The authors verified the data extraction, statistical analyses, interpretation, and final text and take full responsibility for the manuscript.

top_evidence.text: Meta-analysis was conducted only for outcomes reported by at least three non-overlapping primary studies with extractable numerators and denominators. Pooled incidences were estimated using random-effects models for proportions, with variance stabilization for rare events where appropriate. Results were expressed as pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran Q and the I-squared statistic. Heterogeneity was interpreted as low, moderate, substantial, or considerable using conventional thresholds, while acknowledging that I-squared may be unstable in rare-event analyses. We prespecified subgroup exploration by age group, ERCP indication, procedure type, pancreatic duct manipulation or contrast injection, sphincterotomy, and operator or center volume. Formal subgroup meta-analysis was not forced when studies did not provide stratified PEP event counts, because doing so would have required ecological assumptions. These variables were therefore summarized as explanatory domains for heterogeneity and risk. Sensitivity analyses were planned by excluding studies at high risk of bias, studies with unclear adverseevent definitions, and studies with potential cohort overlap. In response to peer review, we also added a post hoc denominator-unit sensitivity summary, separating procedure-level studies from patient-level or first-ERCP-perchild studies and retaining a mixed/unclear category when the source did not permit classification. Risk-factor effect estimates were not pooled when exposure definitions, covariate adjustment, or reporting units differed substantially. These data were summarized narratively and, where appropriate, displayed as reported estimates. ARTICLE IN PRESS Publication bias was assessed visually using funnel plots and statistically using Egger test only for outcomes with at least ten eligible studies. Funnel plots were not generated for rare outcomes with fewer than ten studies because asymmetry tests would be unreliable. All tests were two-sided. For analyses other than Cochran's Q test for heterogeneity, P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For Cochran's Q test, P < 0.10 was considered indicative of potential between-study heterogeneity because this test has limited power when relatively few studies are included. Heterogeneity was interpreted together with I² and τ². AI-assisted tools were used during revision for language editing and formatting checks. The authors verified the data extraction, statistical analyses, interpretation, and final text and take full responsibility for the manuscript.

top_evidence.text: The available evidence suggested that ERCP indication influenced complication patterns. Children undergoing ERCP for acute recurrent or chronic pancreatitis were repeatedly reported to have higher PEP risk than those undergoing ERCP for choledocholithiasis, although the magnitude of association varied by study design, adjustment strategy, and procedural case mix. The overall incidence of post-ERCP complications in children varied across studies because of differences in patient populations, procedural indications, adverse-event definitions, and follow-up. Random-effects pooling was performed for PEP because this outcome had the most consistently extractable numerators and denominators. Figure 2 presents the study-level forest plot for PEP incidence after pediatric ERCP. Bleeding, perforation, and cholangitis were less frequent and were summarized descriptively when study-level event data were sparse or inconsistently reported. PEP : PEP was the most frequent and clinically significant complication associated with pediatric ERCP. In the present synthesis, 15 non-overlapping primary studies contributed extractable PEP event counts, yielding a pooled incidence of 7.3% (95% CI, 5.1% to 10.4%; I-squared = 83.7%) under a random-effects model. Table 1 now reports the study-level numerator, denominator, percentage, denominator unit, and available definition or reporting note for every study contributing to the PEP synthesis. The rows most dependent on percentage backcalculation or source-unit interpretation were rechecked against the original source records for Goetz, Mercier, Perera, and Batibay[24, 60, 63, 72]. ARTICLE IN PRESS The high I-squared value indicates real between-study inconsistency rather than a single uniform pediatric PEP risk. Likely contributors include age distribution, acute recurrent or chronic pancreatitis as the indication, pancreatic duct cannulation or contrast injection, pancreatic sphincterotomy, difficult cannulation, operator and center volume, trainee participation, follow-up windows, and differences in PEP definitions. Denominator unit was another source of variation: some studies reported ERCP procedures, whereas others reported patients or first ERCP per child. Because repeat ERCPs per child were not consistently available, procedure-level data were not converted to patient-level data. In the post hoc denominator-unit summary, procedure-level studies contributed 181 PEP events among 2669 ERCPs (crude rate, 6.8%), patient-level or first-ERCP-per-child studies contributed 20 events among 421 children (4.8%), and the mixed or unclear-denominator study contributed 12 events among 232 observations (5.2%). Heterogeneity persisted after this separation, so the pooled estimate should be interpreted as a contemporary benchmark rather than a single individualized risk estimate. Most pediatric PEP cases are mild and resolve with conservative management, whereas a minority progress to moderate or severe PEP with prolonged hospitalization, systemic inflammatory response, pancreatic necrosis, pseudocyst formation, or rarely mortality[4, 59, 73]. The Atlanta classification, originally developed for adults, is often applied in pediatric settings but has not been fully validated for pediatric post-ERCP pathophysiology [62]. Visual inspection of the PEP funnel plot suggested possible small-study effects, although Egger regression did not show clear statistical evidence of asymmetry (intercept, -1.98; approximate two-sided P = 0.16). This result should be interpreted cautiously because heterogeneity was substantial and denominators were reported as either patients or procedures across studies (Figure 8). Bleeding : Post-ERCP bleeding in children most commonly occurs after endoscopic sphincterotomy (EST). Clinically significant bleeding is uncommon, with an estimated incidence of approximately 0.5%[4]. Bleeding may appear during the procedure, shortly afterward, or several days later. Reported risk factors include coagulopathy, larger sphincterotomy incisions, and vascular anomalies. Most cases respond to endoscopic hemostasis with epinephrine injection or clip placement. Severe or endoscopically refractory bleeding may require angiographic embolization; surgery should be reserved for cases in which less invasive measures fail. Perforation : ERCP-related perforation is rare but potentially life-threatening, with an estimated incidence below 1% in pediatric patients[4]. Risk factors include difficult cannulation, excessive force during guidewire or endoscope advancement, anatomical anomalies, and strictures. A practical concern is device size. Pediatric duodenoscopes have become less available in recent years, so clinicians may need to use adult-sized equipment in small children, which can increase mechanical risk. Early recognition matters: minor perforations may be treated conservatively, whereas larger defects often require surgery. Cholangitis : Post-ERCP cholangitis is a recognized infectious complication, typically resulting from incomplete biliary drainage or procedural contamination. Although its incidence in children is less well-defined than that of PEP, it remains clinically important[63]. Risk factors include persistent biliary obstruction, incomplete stone clearance, and prior biliary surgery. Prophylactic antibiotics are commonly considered, particularly in patients with pre-existing cholangitis or immunocompromised status. Management requires prompt antibiotic therapy and restoration of biliary drainage, which may require repeat ERCP or percutaneous intervention. Other complications : Less common complications of ERCP in children include cholecystitis, bile duct injury or stricture, and events related to sedation or anesthesia[13]. Cholecystitis may arise if the cystic duct is obstructed or manipulated during the procedure. Ductal injury is rare but can lead to later stricture formation. Sedation- and anesthesia-related complications are especially relevant in children because of smaller airway size, higher metabolic demand, and age-specific responses to anesthetic agents. Close monitoring by pediatric anesthesia teams is therefore important for procedural safety[64]. The evidence points to a broad but unevenly reported risk profile for pediatric ERCP. Overall complication rates are usually low, but serious events such as PEP, bleeding, perforation, and cholangitis require close attention. Differences in definitions, follow-up, and reporting explain much of the variability across studies. Better pediatric definitions and prospective datasets are needed before risk estimates for rare outcomes can be pooled with confidence. Risk Factors for Complications Operator background also influenced complication rates. Pediatric series and adult operator-volume data[66, 68, 69] suggest that procedures performed by less experienced operators or outside specialized pediatric endoscopy settings may carry higher procedural risk than procedures performed by experienced pediatric gastroenterologists. These findings support specialized training and referral pathways for complex pediatric ERCP. ARTICLE IN PRESS Identifying risk factors for post-ERCP complications in children helps guide patient selection, preprocedural optimization, and intra-procedural risk mitigation. Across the literature, both patient characteristics and procedural variables were associated with adverse events. Table 2 summarizes major patient- and procedure-related factors associated with higher complication rates, particularly PEP, bleeding, and perforation. To complement this summary, Figure 3 summarizes patient-related and procedure-related risk domains reported across the included literature.

top_evidence.text: The methodological quality and risk of bias of each eligible source were independently assessed by two reviewers using tools appropriate to study design. Disagreements were resolved by consensus, with a third reviewer consulted when needed. Non-randomized primary studies were assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), randomized trials using RoB 2, and prior systematic reviews or meta-analyses using AMSTAR 2[16-18]. Rather than reproducing checklist content, we summarized each study's overall judgment and used these judgments to grade confidence across evidence domains. Risk-of-bias judgments informed the narrative synthesis. Studies with incomplete adverse-event definitions, unclear denominators, overlapping cohorts, or high risk of selection or reporting bias were interpreted cautiously and were not used to support quantitative claims beyond their reported data.

top_evidence.text: Meta-analysis was conducted only for outcomes reported by at least three non-overlapping primary studies with extractable numerators and denominators. Pooled incidences were estimated using random-effects models for proportions, with variance stabilization for rare events where appropriate. Results were expressed as pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran Q and the I-squared statistic. Heterogeneity was interpreted as low, moderate, substantial, or considerable using conventional thresholds, while acknowledging that I-squared may be unstable in rare-event analyses. We prespecified subgroup exploration by age group, ERCP indication, procedure type, pancreatic duct manipulation or contrast injection, sphincterotomy, and operator or center volume. Formal subgroup meta-analysis was not forced when studies did not provide stratified PEP event counts, because doing so would have required ecological assumptions. These variables were therefore summarized as explanatory domains for heterogeneity and risk. Sensitivity analyses were planned by excluding studies at high risk of bias, studies with unclear adverseevent definitions, and studies with potential cohort overlap. In response to peer review, we also added a post hoc denominator-unit sensitivity summary, separating procedure-level studies from patient-level or first-ERCP-perchild studies and retaining a mixed/unclear category when the source did not permit classification. Risk-factor effect estimates were not pooled when exposure definitions, covariate adjustment, or reporting units differed substantially. These data were summarized narratively and, where appropriate, displayed as reported estimates. ARTICLE IN PRESS Publication bias was assessed visually using funnel plots and statistically using Egger test only for outcomes with at least ten eligible studies. Funnel plots were not generated for rare outcomes with fewer than ten studies because asymmetry tests would be unreliable. All tests were two-sided. For analyses other than Cochran's Q test for heterogeneity, P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For Cochran's Q test, P < 0.10 was considered indicative of potential between-study heterogeneity because this test has limited power when relatively few studies are included. Heterogeneity was interpreted together with I² and τ². AI-assisted tools were used during revision for language editing and formatting checks. The authors verified the data extraction, statistical analyses, interpretation, and final text and take full responsibility for the manuscript.

top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: Background Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is increasingly used in children with pancreatobiliary disease, but pediatric adverse-event estimates remain variable. We updated the evidence on post-ERCP adverse events in children, pooled post-ERCP pancreatitis (PEP) incidence when study-level data allowed, and summarized reported risk factors and prevention strategies. Methods We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of English-language literature published from January 2015 to June 2025 in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. Eligible quantitative analyses included non-overlapping pediatric primary studies reporting extractable numerators and denominators for post-ERCP adverse events. Prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses were used for background comparison and reference checking only. Random-effects meta-analysis of proportions was planned for outcomes with at least three eligible studies. Risk-factor and prevention data were summarized narratively when definitions or adjustment strategies were too heterogeneous for pooling. Results Sixty-five sources were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 15 non-overlapping primary studies contributed extractable PEP numerators and denominators for quantitative synthesis. PEP was the most frequent adverse event, with a pooled incidence of approximately 7.3% (95% CI, 5.1% to 10.4%; I-squared = 83.7%). Study-level PEP percentages, denominator units, and available adverse-event definition or reporting notes are now shown in Table 1. Bleeding was uncommon and perforation was rare but clinically important. Recurrent or chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic duct manipulation, pancreatic contrast injection, sphincterotomy, difficult cannulation, younger age, lower procedural volume, and trainee involvement or operator experience were recurring risk domains, although not all studies reported stratified event counts. Pediatric evidence for NSAIDs and prophylactic pancreatic stenting remains limited compared with adult data, and both strategies require childspecific dosing, equipment selection, and contraindication assessment. ARTICLE IN PRESS Conclusions Pediatric ERCP carries measurable adverse-event risk, particularly PEP. The pooled estimate provides a current benchmark, but heterogeneity and inconsistent reporting limit certainty. Standardized pediatric definitions, non-overlapping reporting, and prospective multicenter datasets are needed. Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251084264. Keywords Children; ERCP; Pancreatobiliary disease; Post-procedural complications; Pancreatitis; Systematic review; Meta-analysis; Patient safety

top_evidence.text: The methodological quality and risk of bias of each eligible source were independently assessed by two reviewers using tools appropriate to study design. Disagreements were resolved by consensus, with a third reviewer consulted when needed. Non-randomized primary studies were assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), randomized trials using RoB 2, and prior systematic reviews or meta-analyses using AMSTAR 2[16-18]. Rather than reproducing checklist content, we summarized each study's overall judgment and used these judgments to grade confidence across evidence domains. Risk-of-bias judgments informed the narrative synthesis. Studies with incomplete adverse-event definitions, unclear denominators, overlapping cohorts, or high risk of selection or reporting bias were interpreted cautiously and were not used to support quantitative claims beyond their reported data.
